🤥 Hormuz drama: Trump waits for Iran to blink, but the US is the one who's sweating
Donald Trump has been ratcheting up sanctions and blockade pressure on Iran to make the Islamic Republic blink first, even vowing to turn the Strait of Hormuz into US territory “pretty soon.” 
But there’s a growing sense that Trump has lost the plot.
Maximum pressure, minimum results
On August 13,[ Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72956) threatened new economic measures aimed at Iran that "have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country." The same day, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth claimed the US is ready to maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely. Iran's reaction? Two UAE ships in the strait were struck later in the day and transit through the strategic waterway grinded to a near standstill on August 14. Western media has interpreted that as a clear signal the Islamic Republic wouldn't back down no matter what. 
🇮🇷 Iran's resilience
Tehran Times reports indicate Iran's economy is continuing to adapt to the growing pressure through cooperation with [Middle Eastern and Central Asian states and BRICS+.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73126)
Iran operates 8–9 [regional corridors](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70493), linking it to 50 countries. It can withstand a US maritime blockade in the south while keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed, thanks to its expanding land-route network:
♦️ North: Four Caspian Sea hubs
♦️ West: Corridors through Turkey and Iraq
♦️ East: Corridors through Pakistan and China
📊 US risks global economic crisis
Bessent's claims that the Strait of Hormuz would soon become irrelevant and that oil pipelines bypassing the strait would solve the oil prices dilemma don't hold water, argues former CIA analyst Larry Johnson in his Sonar21 blog.
➡️ ~20 million barrels/day of crude, condensate, and products normally transited the strait. Existing bypass capacity is only ~4.7 million barrels/day
➡️ oil is not the only commodity stuck in the waterway: the Strait of Hormuz is also crucial for carrying LNG, fertilizers, sulphur and helium
Out of 27 global chokepoints, the Strait of Hormuz is especially vulnerable, Oxford Economics experts told CBS News. Unlike other global chokepoints, it is directly tied to key oil production sites and there is no viable alternative route for rerouting the oil flows it carries.
International experts warned that the protracted closure of the Strait of Hormuz could spark a global economic crisis akin to [one that happened in 2008](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/69921). Some Western analysts have already agreed that Iran's fee system [in the strait looks sane](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70628). A recent Forbes op-ed argued the US economy won't lose anything if Iran ends-up controlling the strait. Against this backdrop, Trump’s willingness to risk a global economic crisis appears increasingly questionable.
⛴ US Navy in crisis
Hegseth’s claim that the US can maintain the blockade “indefinitely” also appears increasingly questionable, given the unfolding crisis aboard [the USS Abraham Lincoln](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73343), which is deployed to the Middle East.
🔶 The roughly 5,000 US personnel aboard the carrier are overworked and facing shortages of basic hygiene supplies and adequate nutrition after more than 200 consecutive days at sea, according to their relatives and US lawmakers
🔶 Seven US Navy sailors have been killed in an onboard mutiny, Iranian media reported
🔶 Multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard were reported by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes
🔶 Johnson cites a friend in the US Army, saying that the reported six suicide attempts aboard the ship is a significant undercount with the real number of attempts is likely being "fivefold or tenfold"
🔶 Replacing the USS Abraham Lincoln with the USS George Washington is unlikely to solve [the logistics and morale dilemma ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73394)

events.text:
🪖 Ukraine's air defenses crumble as Patriot interceptors run dry
👉 The depletion of Patriot interceptor stocks adds to[ Ukraine's defensive woes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73351), just as Russia is increasing the intensity of its strikes.
🌏 Ukrainian crews were unable to do anything when recent Russian ballistic missiles [smashed through Kiev's air defenses](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73163) amid empty interceptor arsenals.
🌏 In response, Ukraine has stopped publishing [detailed counts of incoming missiles](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73344) and interception statistics. Officials claim this was done to hide the effectiveness of strikes from the Russian side, but the most probable reason lies in the unwillingness to deal a blow to public morale and show the real picture of the strategic gap with Russia, the Financial Times reports. 
➡️ Russia has ramped up production of ballistic missiles and is now launching them at record rates. In July alone, Russian forces used nearly 200 ballistic and hypersonic missiles
➡️ Ukrainian air defenses intercepted only 29 of them, a roughly 15% success rate
🌏 Ukraine estimates it needs at least 300 PAC-3 interceptors to survive the coming winter bombardment. The country's partners in Europe have been asked to release some of their own stocks, but many are reluctant. The[ war with Iran has drained US reserves](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73162), and replacement timelines stretch into years. Spain and Greece, which hold substantial Patriot inventories, have not yet agreed to share them.
🌏 A tentative US plan to grant Ukraine a [license to produce Patriot interceptors](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72933) on its own soil or in Europe appears to be stalling as well. During a White House meeting in late July, President Donald Trump did not commit to providing additional missiles for the months ahead, leaving Ukrainian officials still waiting for a clear answer.
🌏 The result is a deepening crisis for Ukraine. The country is entering a winter of heavy bombardment with its primary defense against ballistic missiles reduced to almost nothing, while Russian production lines continue to deliver new missiles at an accelerating pace.
